name: Bell's Theorem
statement: No physical theory based on local hidden variables can reproduce all the statistical predictions of quantum mechanics.
meaning: Bell’s theorem shows that quantum mechanics is fundamentally incompatible with "local realism" — the idea that particles have definite pre-existing properties and that influences cannot travel faster than light. It proves that any theory obeying locality and realism must satisfy a mathematical constraint (a Bell inequality) that quantum mechanics predicts will be violated.
mechanism: Bell derived an inequality that any local hidden-variable theory must obey for correlations between measurements on entangled particle pairs, then showed quantum mechanics predicts correlations exceeding that bound. Experimental violation of the inequality thus rules out local hidden variables as an explanation for entanglement, as originally raised by the 1935 Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox.

examples.text: John Stewart Bell published "On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox" in Physics Physique Fizika in 1964, introducing the theorem; it drew almost no attention for its first several years.
John Clauser and Stuart Freedman performed the first experimental test of a Bell-type inequality in 1972, observing violations consistent with quantum mechanics rather than local hidden variables.

Alain Aspect and colleagues conducted more rigorous tests in 1982 using time-varying analyser settings, closing loopholes present in earlier experiments and more convincingly confirming quantum predictions over local realism.

whyItMatters: Bell’s theorem underlies the modern understanding of quantum entanglement and nonlocality, and technologies built on verified entanglement — quantum cryptography and computing — rest on the experimentally confirmed violation of Bell inequalities.
limits: Experimental tests historically faced loopholes (detection efficiency, locality/timing) that in principle could rescue local hidden-variable models; these were closed simultaneously only in 2015 by three independent groups. Some interpretations, such as superdeterminism or many-worlds, preserve locality or determinism by rejecting other assumptions, but remain minority positions.
misreadings: Bell’s theorem is often misreported as proving faster-than-light signalling is possible; in fact it rules out local hidden variables while entanglement still cannot be used to transmit information faster than light.
origin: Proved by physicist John Stewart Bell in 1964, building on the 1935 Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox; experimentally confirmed starting with Clauser and Freedman (1972) and Aspect (1982).

sources.text: Bell, J. S. (1964). "On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen paradox." Physics Physique Fizika 1(3), 195-200 — the paper proving the inequality.
